blocks.content: The SQL Joins module covered how to combine data that already lives in separate, well structured tables. This new module, Relational Database Design, steps back to the more fundamental question, what actually makes something a table in the first place, and what do rows and columns actually represent.

This topic covers what a table, row, and column each genuinely mean in a relational database, how a table differs from a plain spreadsheet even though the two look superficially similar, and the practical naming and typing decisions that shape a well designed table.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513567-317613110.png
1. What a Table Actually Is

A table is a structured collection of data about one specific kind of thing, customers, orders, products, each table is dedicated to exactly one entity type, keeping every customer in a customers table and every order in a separate orders table.

Suppose you build a small online store. You genuinely need a place to store customer information and a separate place to store order information, a table gives each of these its own consistent, well defined structure rather than mixing everything together.
2. Rows Represent One Instance
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513567-153053616.png

Each row in a table represents exactly one instance of that table entity type, one specific customer, one specific order, one specific product, every row shares the same structure, the same set of columns, but holds different actual values.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513943-522567028.png
3. Columns Represent One Attribute
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513944-693377861.png

A column captures exactly one attribute shared across every row in the table, a customers table might have an id column, a name column, an email column, and a created_at column, every row in that table has a value, or explicitly no value, for each of these columns.
This consistency is what makes a table genuinely useful, you always know exactly what kind of information to expect in each column, regardless of which specific row you are looking at.

4. A Worked Example
Building a customers table from scratch
blocks.text: Building a customers table from scratch

blocks.content: Suppose your online store needs to track customers. You decide the attributes that matter are a unique identifier, a name, an email address, and the date they signed up, this directly becomes your table design.

Every row you insert into this table going forward must fit this exact structure, a value, or an explicit null, for each of these four columns, this is the enforced consistency a relational table provides.
5. Choosing the Right Column Data Type
blocks.text: 5. Choosing the Right Column Data Type

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513945-714683594.png
blocks.alt: Choosing the Right Column Data Type

blocks.content: Every column has a declared data type, INTEGER for whole numbers, VARCHAR for variable length text, DATE for calendar dates, BOOLEAN for true or false values, this type is enforced by the database itself, an attempt to insert text into an INTEGER column simply fails.

{"headers":["Data Type","Typical Use"],"rows":[["INTEGER","Whole numbers, identifiers, counts"],["VARCHAR","Variable length text like names or emails"],["DATE","Calendar dates without a time component"],["BOOLEAN","True or false values"]]}
6. Tables vs Spreadsheets
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513945-130796808.png

A table looks superficially similar to a spreadsheet, rows and columns of data, but a spreadsheet cell can hold anything, text one row and a number the next, a database column enforces its declared type consistently across every single row, this enforcement is what lets a database reliably query, sort, and calculate against that column.

blocks.title: This enforcement is not a limitation, it is the whole point
blocks.content: A spreadsheet flexibility to hold anything in any cell is exactly what makes large scale, reliable querying difficult, a database table strict typing is what makes millions of rows queryable in milliseconds.
7. Naming Tables and Columns Well
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513945-436015960.png

A column named data1 or val tells a future reader nothing about what it actually holds, a column named order_total or signup_date is immediately understandable, clear naming is a small habit that pays off enormously once a database grows past a handful of tables.

Table names conventionally use a plural noun, customers rather than customer, since a table holds many rows of that entity type, this convention, while not universally enforced, is common enough that following it makes a schema easier for other people to read.

blocks.title: A consistent naming convention matters more than which one you pick
blocks.content: Whether a team chooses plural table names or singular ones, snake_case columns or camelCase, the specific convention matters far less than applying it consistently across every table in the schema.
8. Common Mistakes
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438513946-565221652.png

["Mixing multiple unrelated entity types into a single table instead of giving each its own table","Choosing a data type that is too loose, storing dates or numbers as plain text with no type enforcement","Using vague column names that require guessing what the column actually contains","Confusing a table structure with a spreadsheet, and expecting a column to hold mixed data types"]

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["A table holds one entity type, with each row representing one instance and each column representing one attribute shared across all rows","A database column enforces a declared data type consistently, unlike a freeform spreadsheet cell","Clear table and column naming pays off significantly as a schema grows in size and complexity","The next topic, Primary Key, covers exactly how a table uniquely identifies each individual row"]
